And every day he would send an envoy and say to the Tatars:
"Watch and wake up from your sleep,
for behold, the Egyptian has approached with a great force."
And in this way, again, the Parwana lied and would say to the Tatars:
"Leo is doing you a favor,
and instead of food and drink,
he is sending you news!"
And on account of this, they did not believe King Leo's word.
And that Parwana would prepare a feast for them every day and get them drunk,
until Friday,
the sixteenth of Nisan of that same year 1588
[158a] of the Greeks,
on which the Egyptians attacked the Mongols
and found them drunk and stupefied with wine.
And with difficulty was each one of them able to mount his steed.
And because it was not in their law to flee before engaging the enemy,
they engaged the Egyptians
and were broken before them.
And in this defeat, two great Tatar chiefs were killed:
one, indeed, was Toghu,
and the other was Tudan the champion (athlete).
And although there were three thousand Iberians (Georgians) with the Tatars,
two thousand were killed after the great endurance they showed,
and they struck down many of the Egyptians;
and one thousand of the Iberians escaped.
And of the Mongols, about five thousand fell in battle.
And when the Parwana saw that the Tatars were broken,
he took the Sultan and fled to the fortress of Dawqiya (Duqiyyah?).
And Bunduqdar, the lord of Egypt,
went and pitched his tents near Caesarea in a place called Kayqubad,
and he remained there fifteen days.
And he also entered Caesarea once
and sat upon the throne of the Sultan.
And he did not harm any of the common people, nor did he plunder;
rather, his soldiers took everything at a fair price,
to the point that they even bought fodder for their horses.
For he said:
"I have not come to destroy this land,
but to free its lord from the servitude of the Tatars."
Now Abaqa, the King of Kings,
as soon as he heard the news,
marshaled the forces that were prepared,
and set his face toward the territory of the Romans.
And when Bunduqdar knew that his army was not able [to withstand him],
